The endset temperatures point down to indicate that the real liquidus must be below this temperature. The nature of these bounds in relation to the true equilibrium liquidus requires some explanation. At compositions approaching the pure component, the endset will tend to overshoot the liquidus temperature to ever greater extents. This is because the true two-phase region is quite small and the amount of time required to transfer heat into the sample begins to exceed the total time to heat the sensor past the liquidus temperature. Also, in the more dilute samples, the degree of undercooling tends to increase. Given the presence of many external nucleation sites (the crucible wall for instance), the undercooling is not expected 6 to vary as significantly in these experiments as does the endset. Given these considerations, the bounding values for the liquidus will be wide though the required convergence of the true liquidus with the solidus line at pure uranium adds additional constraint. Interpretation of boundary temperatures with composition becomes difficult close to the peritectic liquidus for two reasons. First, at these compositions, the equilibrium volume fraction of Mo is quite small, BCC leading to a commensurately small thermal signal. Secondly, the Mo liquidus rises very steeply in this BCC region, quickly exceeding the temperatures accessible in the experimental equipment. Therefore, the endset values tend to become somewhat meaningless and the peritectic invariant temperature becomes more difficult to identify. These are the primary reasons for a lower confidence level for reinterpretation of the peritectic temperature. That said, post-mortem microscopy from the experiments conducted here provide valuable insight for phase boundaries, especially in the region of the peritectic liquidus intersection.
